1.why: Dangling-modifier set: C is the only option whose subject is an active human agent (the committee); A/B/D are passive, expletive, or abstract-noun subjects that cannot be modified by an introductory participle.

2.why: their/its/they're/it's - nothing in the option set reveals the antecedent's number; betting on the singular possessive as the most common key in this family.

3.why: Of the four, 'to satisfy' is the bare infinitive that fits the widest range of frames; D is a finite clause (run-on bait) and A adds a preposition.

4.why: Agreement set with a lone singular against three plurals; if number is the tested axis the minority-number option must be the key.

5.why: Modifier set: C is the only option whose bare subject is the mural itself; A shifts to visitors, B uses an expletive, D buries the mural in a possessive.

6.why: Pure tense set; betting on the aspectually marked present-perfect over the simple forms.

7.why: Tense set built around a past-perfect trigger; 'had cleared' is the marked form the item exists to test.

8.why: Lone singular ('is') against three plural forms - minority-number bet.

9.why: Lone plural ('are') against three singular forms - minority-number bet, applied in the same direction as items 4/8/10/18/23.

10.why: Lone plural ('were') against three singular forms - minority-number bet.

11.why: comma/colon/semicolon/'that is': the presence of an explanatory connector as a distractor suggests an explanation follows a complete clause, which is colon territory.

12.why: Tense set with one non-finite bait and one modal; betting on the marked past-perfect progressive.

13.why: they/and it/which/it - two bare pronouns differing only in number plus two connector variants; no visible antecedent, betting singular.

14.why: one/you/he/they - pronoun-consistency set with no visible antecedent; 'one' is the form these sets are usually built around.

15.why: Every option is a mark plus the verb 'are', so the following word is the predicate - no punctuation may separate subject from verb, leaving the unpunctuated option.

16.why: ', but' is the only well-formed coordination: ', ' alone splices, ' but,' misplaces the comma after the conjunction, and '; but' double-marks the join.

17.why: One present, one future, one past, one present-perfect; betting on the marked perfect form per the same rule used on 6/7/12.

18.why: Lone singular ('is') against three plural forms - minority-number bet.

19.why: their/its/it's/there - homophone set with no visible antecedent; same singular-possessive bet as item 2.

20.why: C is nonsense bait and D lacks an object, but A (passive participle, object as main subject) and B (perfect participle, archaeologist as main subject) are both legal without the sentence; betting on the passive.

21.why: 'flour' opens what is plainly a list after a complete clause, so the colon is the only legal mark; C's 'being' and D's '; and' are standard over-punctuation baits.

22.why: 'nurses's' is never legal in any sentence and exists only as the malformed twin of the tested form, which points to the correctly written plural possessive.

23.why: Lone singular ('is') against three plural forms - minority-number bet.

24.why: Modifier set: C is the only option whose subject is the person; A makes the earthquake the subject, B the seismic data, D an expletive - all three would dangle an introductory participle about Dr. Halloran.
